n: About fourteen months after his call (about 592 BC), Judah’s elders in exile are sitting in Ezekiel’s house when God’s power falls on him. Chapters 8–11 form one long vision.

f.w: the sixth year, in the sixth month
f.g: Of King Jehoiachin’s exile—about September 592 BC.

f.w: the elders of Judah sat before me

n: Ezekiel sees a fiery, radiant figure like the one on the throne in chapter 1.

A hand grabs him by the hair, and the Spirit carries him in vision to Jerusalem’s temple. There, at the north gate, stands an idol called “the image of jealousy” because it provokes God’s jealous love for his people.

f.w: took me by a lock of mine head

f.g: Perhaps an image of the goddess Asherah, like the one King Manasseh once set in the temple.

n: God’s glory is still present in the temple, just as Ezekiel saw it in the plain—for now. These chapters trace its slow departure.

f.w: according to the vision that I saw in the plain

n: Looking north, Ezekiel sees the idol standing at the gate by the altar—right at the entrance to God’s house.

f.g: A northern gate of the inner court, near the great altar.

n: These abominations are driving God away from his own sanctuary. “But you will see even worse.” The vision builds in four escalating scenes.

f.w: that I should go far off from my sanctuary

n: At the entrance to the court Ezekiel sees a hole in the wall.
Told to dig through it, he finds a hidden door—secret sin concealed inside the house of God.

f.g: An image of exposing what is hidden.

n: He is told to go in and see the wicked things being done there.
Inside, the walls are carved with unclean creatures and idols—likely Egyptian-style animal gods—that the law forbade Israel to worship.
Seventy elders—the very number Moses appointed to lead Israel—are offering incense to these images. Among them is Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan, from a family that had otherwise been faithful.

f.g: Josiah’s scribe; his sons supported Jeremiah.

n: They worship in the dark, each in his own room of images, telling themselves that the Lord doesn’t see and has abandoned the land. Secret sin often begins with the belief that God isn’t watching.

f.g: Rooms decorated with idolatrous images; also suggests their private thoughts.

n: “Turn again, and you will see greater abominations.”

f.g: The escalation continues to a third scene.

n: At the north gate of the temple, women sit weeping for Tammuz, a Mesopotamian fertility god whose death was mourned each summer.

f.g: Babylonian Dumuzi, a god of vegetation believed to die and revive with the seasons; the fourth month of the Jewish calendar still bears his name.

n: “Have you seen this? You will see still greater abominations.”

f.g: God asks Ezekiel to fully take in what he is seeing.

n: The worst scene, in the inner court right at the temple door: about twenty-five men turn their backs on the Lord’s house and bow to the rising sun in the east—an act of total rejection.

f.w: with their backs toward the temple of the LORD
between the porch and the altar

n: Idolatry isn’t a minor thing: it goes hand in hand with filling the land with violence. “They put the branch to their nose” is an obscure idiom, probably a pagan ritual gesture or an insulting gesture toward God.

f.w: they put the branch to their nose
f.g: Meaning uncertain; possibly a ritual act in sun worship, or an obscene insult to God.

n: Therefore God will act without pity. Even if they cry loudly to him, he will not answer—prayer without repentance does not move heaven.

f.w: though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them
